doc.title: Toots Thielemans — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Drummers: Bill Clark, Steve Gadd and Elvin Jones
summary: He recalls the feel with Bill Clark and Steve Gadd and a J.J. Johnson date with Elvin Jones.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Did you ever develop this kind of relationship with any particular drummers?

Bill Clark. That was when Shearing, with Shearing. And after hours, sometimes, even in Detroit that I remember very clearly. We went… he had the phone book in his room, right. May I use your phone book? “Come on, sister. That was [his?] sister,” you know the… I’m kidding, you know, but a black man saying sister, anyway… [laughs]
Come on, sister. And we played. And when the groove started to move nicely, he said [inaudible], would stay like that as long as you play, you know. [imitating] That’s Bill.
And with Steve Gadd, also, was wonderful. And I played… No, I can’t say I played much with… there’s people like Roy Haynes, Maxwell [inaudible]. No, I really wasn’t with Shearing, you know.
I have a list of some of the drummers that you played with. Dannie Richmond. Of course you mentioned Arthur Taylor earlier.
And Elvin Jones. Ed Thigpen. Oh… you want to talk about Elvin. [laughs]
Oh, Elvin. Yeah. That was a [inaudible] [Gelder?], at the studio in Jersey. Oh, [bloomy?], we were together. And Elvin… It was a date for J. J. Johnson, I think.
And he played so… He [sounded?]… Oh, I’m going to remember to do it with my little harmonica [inaudible]. And it sounded so light. No [more?] he could blow a house

away, but it was right there then. It’s a matter of feeling together, and there’s no way you may be playing with this, the greatest drummer in magazines and write-ups, but if you’re… if your pulse is not the same, you don’t feel together. [laughs]
And that’s what, you know… [imitating] Whatever he did, it was there, you know. And you know what I’m talking about.
